title: Follow that man
hook: Zeno asks the bookseller where men like Socrates can be found, and Crates the Cynic walks past
carry: nothing terrible has happened to you

segments.voice: Yesterday: Zeno's shipwreck. A fortune lost at sea, and a merchant hooked on a book about Socrates in a bookshop.
screen: `ZENO'S SHIPWRECK — I SAILED WELL WHEN I WAS WRECKED.`

segments.voice: Zeno looks up from the page. Socrates has been dead for generations, so he asks the bookseller: where can I find men like this? Real ones. Alive. And right then, as if the story had been waiting for its cue, a strange figure walks past the shop door. The bookseller points at him and says three words. Follow that man.
screen: `ZENO LOOKS UP FROM THE PAGE.` → `WHERE CAN I FIND MEN LIKE THIS?` → `A STRANGE FIGURE WALKS PAST.`

segments.voice: The man walking past was Crates, a Cynic philosopher. The Cynics were the punk rockers of ancient Greece. They owned almost nothing, slept in public, said exactly what they thought, and mocked anything fake. The name comes from the Greek for dog-like, because they lived as openly as dogs. Crates had been born rich, in Thebes, and given his wealth away. Ancient writers say people called him the door-opener, because he walked into any house he liked and gave the family advice, and they were glad to see him. A woman named Hipparchia, from a wealthy family, fell in love with him, chose his life of the road over her comfortable one, and became a philosopher in her own right. So Zeno followed, and became Crates's student. But Zeno was shy, and the Cynics were shameless on purpose. Diogenes Laërtius tells this story. Crates hands Zeno a pot of lentil soup and tells him to carry it through a busy part of Athens. Zeno, embarrassed, tries to hide it under his cloak. Crates cracks the pot with his staff. Soup runs down Zeno's legs. Zeno runs. And Crates calls after him, roughly: why are you running, my little Phoenician? Nothing terrible has happened to you. Embarrassment, Crates was saying, isn't harm. And look at how it all began. A curious question, asked out loud. A stranger walking past. And the nerve to get up from a bookseller's bench and follow him out the door.
screen: `THE CYNICS: DOG-LIKE, AND PROUD.` · `CRATES, THE DOOR-OPENER.` · `A POT OF LENTIL SOUP.` · `EMBARRASSMENT ISN'T HARM.` · then, large: `FOLLOW THAT MAN.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the breath settle, then ask Zeno's question in your own words: where can I find more of this? Let one curiosity come, a subject, a skill, a kind of person you'd like to learn from. Then picture the bookseller pointing, and notice where the finger goes: a book, a class, a person you could ask.
Crates. The Cynic who walked past a bookshop, and the man a shipwrecked merchant got up to follow.
Your line: nothing terrible has happened to you. Spilled soup is only spilled soup. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: In the ancient schools, people learned philosophy by attaching themselves to a living teacher and following them about; many people today still seek out a teacher or a community to learn from in person.

fork.setup: you're Crates. your shy new student is hiding a pot of lentil soup under his cloak as you cross a crowded street. what do you do?
options: let him hide it. he'll learn in time.
crack the pot with your staff.
take the pot and carry it yourself.
fork.reveal: Crates breaks the pot, the soup runs down Zeno's legs, Zeno runs, and Crates calls: nothing terrible has happened to you.

original.note: Greek, kynikos: dog-like, from kyon, dog. The name of the Cynic philosophers, and the root of English cynic.

trapdoor: what you thought: a bookseller's throwaway line.
what it means: a curious question asked out loud, and the nerve to get up and follow the answer.
what a scholar hears: Diogenes Laërtius 7.2–3 gives the bookshop and the soup; 6.86 calls Crates the door-opener, and 6.96–98 tells of Hipparchia.
recall: the feeling nobody is with you

chat.says: Why did Crates crack the pot of soup Zeno was carrying?
options: To show shy Zeno that being embarrassed isn't the same as being harmed.
Because Cynics owned nothing, so Zeno wasn't allowed even a pot of soup.
To punish Zeno for following him out of the bookshop without asking.
chat.meaning: Crates called after him: nothing terrible has happened to you. Embarrassment, he was saying, isn't harm.

Crates.meaning: a Cynic philosopher, born rich in Thebes, who gave his wealth away

Cynics.meaning: Greek philosophers who owned almost nothing and mocked anything fake

Hipparchia.meaning: a woman from a wealthy family who became a Cynic philosopher

Thebes.meaning: an ancient Greek city, Crates's birthplace

Diogenes Laërtius.meaning: an ancient writer who collected lives of the Greek philosophers

sources.ref: Diogenes Laërtius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers 7.2–3 (the bookshop; the lentil soup)

notes: Socrates died 399 BCE; Zeno arrived in Athens c. 312 BCE, so the script says 'nearly ninety years'. Confirm Zeno's arrival date.
The soup story (DL 7.3): Crates breaks the pot with his staff; 'Why run away, my little Phoenician? Nothing terrible has befallen you.' Paraphrased.
'Punk rockers of ancient Greece' is a modern analogy; a Keeper may prefer something else.
